$comment: Controlled vocabulary of skeletal and soft-tissue attachment sites. Every `attachments` reference in data/muscles-*.json resolves to an `id` here. Three things this buys that a free-string list did not: (1) `partOf` gives the bone-first browse a drill-down (pectoral girdle -> scapula -> acromion); (2) `presence` records where an element is absent, so the interface can show that a muscle's attachment had to move rather than silently dropping the row; (3) `correlate: true` marks sites that leave a recognisable osteological trace, which is the entry point for fossil reconstruction. Presence statements are sourced; where a source is not yet attached the claim is standard comparative anatomy and flagged `sourced: false`.

presence.note: A therian novelty. Incipient in monotremes, which is why the monotreme shoulder is the readable intermediate: it divides the ancestral supracoracoideus field into supraspinatus and infraspinatus.
Cartilaginous dorsal extension of the scapula. Its loss in mammals shifts several axio-appendicular insertions onto the scapular border itself.

All that remains of the coracoid in therians, fused to the scapula. Muscles that arose from the coracoid bone in other tetrapods — biceps brachii and coracobrachialis — arise from this process instead.

Lost as an independent ossification in therians, surviving only as the coracoid process of the scapula. This single loss forces the origin of the supracoracoideus onto the lateral scapula and removes the coracoid head of the subcoracoscapularis — the clearest case in the dataset of an attachment moving because its bone disappeared.
Carries the origin of the procoracohumeralis — the amphibian name for what amniotes call the deltoideus clavicularis. The muscle is renamed for the bone, not for any change in the muscle.
Dermal element linking the pectoral girdle to the skull in fishes. Its loss along the tetrapod stem is what frees the girdle from the head and permits a neck.
Reduced or absent in many cursorial mammals; fused into the furcula in birds.
Retained in monotremes, which is a large part of why the monotreme pectoralis has a more extensive origin than the therian one.
Chen et al. (2025) score this region across crown birds in an osteological character matrix; their scoring conventions are the reference for how these elements are delimited here.

Carries both the pectoralis and the supracoracoideus. The whole flight apparatus is powered from below the centre of mass because the supracoracoideus tendon is redirected dorsally through the foramen triosseum. Chen et al. (2025) score this region across crown birds in an osteological character matrix; their scoring conventions are the reference for how these elements are delimited here.

The single most useful osteological correlate in the pectoral appendage. Its presence and shape is the primary evidence for reconstructing the pectoralis, supracoracoideus and deltoid complex in fossil taxa.
Common origin of the extensor (dorsal-mass, radial-innervated) forearm musculature throughout Tetrapoda.

Common origin of the flexor (ventral-mass) forearm musculature. Diogo & Molnar (2014) follow Sigurdsen & Bolt (2009) in reidentifying the salamander 'ulnar condyle' of Francis (1934) as the entepicondyle.
Insertion of the triceps throughout Tetrapoda; a reliable fossil indicator of elbow extensor leverage.

Expansion of the iliac blade along the synapsid stem tracks the enlargement of the iliofemoralis/gluteal field and is central to Bishop & Pierce's (2024) argument that erect posture was acquired late.

The best single fossil-muscle landmark in the vertebrate skeleton. It carries the caudofemoralis, so its size reads directly as femoral-retractor power, and its independent reduction in birds and loss in mammals marks two separate departures from tail-driven locomotion. Godoy et al. (2016) identify it in the baurusuchid Pissarrachampsa as a rough convexity continuing distally as a faint ridge — much less prominent than the crocodylian condition.
Independently acquired in birds and mammals; a sesamoid in the knee extensor tendon.
Proximal tibial crest receiving the knee extensor tendon; prominent in archosaurs.
No tetrapod counterpart. The tetrapod autopod is a novelty rather than a transformed radial series — see Diogo et al. (2016) on the distal tendon primordium.
Cartilaginous plate in the fenestra ovalis. Target of the opercularis, a pectoral-girdle muscle that inserts on the ear — the amphibian substrate-vibration pathway.
Configuration of the temporal openings constrains adductor mandibulae volume and orientation; the primary osteological handle on jaw muscle reconstruction in fossils.

elements.label: Meckel's cartilage
elements.transformation: The endoskeletal core of the lower jaw, present in every jawed vertebrate. In chondrichthyans it IS the lower jaw; in bony fishes and tetrapods a series of dermal bones ensheaths it, and it persists inside them.

presence.note: The reduced first (mandibular) gill slit. Its pouch is the ancestor of the tympanic cavity, and the region keeps trigeminal innervation throughout.

Cartilage at the corner of the mouth carrying the levator anguli oris. In colubroid snakes it is elaborated into the venom gland, which is why parts of the levator anguli oris there insert on the gland rather than the plate.
Rostral origin of the adductor internus in anurans, medial to the eye.
Tendinous sheet receiving much of the adductor complex in turtles.
Endoskeletal pectoral girdle of fishes, bearing the articular process for the fin. It is the element that becomes the separate scapula and coracoid of tetrapods.
The fin articulation on the scapulocoracoid. Diogo et al. (2016) use it as the landmark separating dorsal (adductor) from ventral (abductor) muscle origins — the fish equivalent of the glenoid.
Ramus of the fish pelvic plate. Diogo et al. (2016) record several pelvic fin muscles arising from its dorsal, medial and caudolateral faces.
The proximo-distal series of the metapterygial axis. Its first and second elements correspond to the tetrapod stylopod and zeugopod; the pronator and supinator series attach segmentally along it.
Principal origin surface for the adductor mandibulae in taxa with an open or emarginated temporal region.
The sole bone of the therian lower jaw; elsewhere one of several, with the postdentary series carrying part of the adductor insertion.
Major adductor insertion surface in non-mammalian tetrapods.

elements.label: Angular / ectotympanic
elements.transformation: A postdentary dermal bone that becomes the ring supporting the mammalian tympanic membrane.

elements.label: Articular / malleus
elements.transformation: The ossified posterior end of Meckel's cartilage. It meets the quadrate at the jaw joint in non-mammals and becomes the malleus in mammals — the partner of the quadrate/incus, moving into the ear together with it.

presence.note: Incorporated into the mammalian middle ear or lost as the dentary takes over the jaw joint.
Ventral tubercle of the avian proximal humerus; receives the coracobrachialis caudalis.

elements.label: Hyomandibula / stapes
elements.transformation: One element throughout. The hyomandibula braces the jaw joint against the braincase in fishes; with the tetrapod jaw suspension it is freed and becomes the sound-conducting columella, and the stapes of mammals. The muscle acting on it followed it the whole way — the depressor hyomandibulae of a shark is the stapedius of a mammal, still on the facial nerve.

elements.label: Palatoquadrate / quadrate
elements.transformation: The upper jaw cartilage of the first pharyngeal arch. Its posterior end ossifies as the quadrate and carries the jaw joint in non-mammals; in mammals it leaves the jaw entirely and becomes the incus, which is why the mammalian jaw joint is squamosal-dentary instead of quadrate-articular.

presence.note: A distinct cervical series requires the girdle to be freed from the skull, which happens with the loss of the cleithrum along the tetrapod stem.

The sacrum is a tetrapod novelty: fishes have no vertebrae fused to a pelvic girdle, because the pelvic fin girdle floats free of the axial skeleton. Fusing them is what lets a hindlimb transmit thrust to the body.
Replaced by the urostyle in anurans and shortened to the pygostyle in birds — both associated with caudofemoralis reduction.
The connective-tissue sheet dividing epaxial from hypaxial musculature. It is the boundary that defines the two, and it is marked by the split of the spinal nerve into dorsal and ventral rami.
Segmental connective-tissue partitions between myomeres. Tetrapod axial muscles lose strict segmental septation as they reorganise into longitudinal tracts.

elements.label: Pygostyle
elements.transformation: The distal caudal vertebrae fused into a single plate.

presence.note: Fused post-sacral rod replacing the anuran tail. Its rigidity is part of the saltatory apparatus.

A preaxial element medial to digit I. In anurans it carries its own musculature — adductor pollicis, a contrahens, flexores breves profundi slips — so it behaves as a digit even though it is not one. Relevant to the position-versus-identity argument: anurans lost digit 1 yet the preaxial muscles found something to attach to.
Pedal counterpart of the prepollex, with its own abductor and flexor musculature in anurans.
Blotto et al. (2020) refer the origin of most anuran intrinsic hand muscles to the fused distal carpal 3-4-5.
An anuran carpal element receiving the extensor carpi radialis tendon.
Elongated with the fibulare into the anuran tarsal segment that lengthens the jumping limb.

elements.label: Tibiotarsus

presence.note: Fused tibia and proximal tarsals in birds.

elements.transformation: Tibia fused with the proximal tarsals (astragalus and calcaneum).

elements.label: Tarsometatarsus

presence.note: Fused distal tarsals and metatarsals II-IV in birds. Its proximal dorsal tuberosities are the insertion correlate for the m. tibialis cranialis.

elements.transformation: Distal tarsals fused with metatarsals II-IV. Metatarsal I remains free, so the metatarsal series is not wholly absorbed.

presence.note: Insertion correlate for the pedal extensor series; recognisable in fossils.
Origin correlate for the m. interosseus dorsalis digiti II.
The varanid trochanter receiving the caudofemoralis; homologous with the fourth trochanter of archosaurs.
Where present, carries much of the abductor superficialis origin in teleosts.
The anteriormost ray, served by its own arrector muscles in teleosts — the first differentiation out of the abductor-arrector anlage.
Origin surface of the teleost adductor mandibulae.
Occupied by section Aω of the teleost adductor mandibulae.
Its hollow carries the origin of the extensor digitorum brevis superficialis in Caiman.
Landmark on the fibular shaft; the fibularis longus arises distal to it.

Fine striae, longitudinal or parallel to the metatarsal long axis, marking the origins of the deep pedal series. Pereyra et al. (2024) identify these as pedal muscle correlates for the first time; because they vary little between crocodylian species they are usable on fossil archosaurs.
The rib-bearing facet on the transverse process. Origin of the levator costae in varanids, which is one of the two muscles connecting each rib independently to the vertebral column.
Cieri (2018) reports three to four in most varanids examined.
Reach the sternum by a sternal portion of calcified cartilage; three in most varanids.
Bony vertebral portion plus a costal cartilage that does not reach the sternum.

The ossified ascending process of the palatoquadrate. Werneburg & Maier (2019) show it forms the secondary lateral braincase wall in cryptodire turtles, while pleurodires build that wall from the descending process of the parietal instead, having no extended ascending process to ossify.
Its reduction is one of four character complexes Werneburg & Maier (2019) tie to the akinetic turtle skull.

Werneburg & Preuschoft (2024) treat the temporal bars as struts resisting the compressive and tensile stresses of biting; the pattern of openings between them follows from where those stresses run, rather than being an arbitrary taxonomic character.
Y-shaped cartilage projecting forward from the anterior margin of the pubis. Anchors the anterior continuation of the rectus abdominis and receives the m. ypsiloideus.

Origin of the caudofemoralis and of the tail-to-girdle muscles. In Taricha the caudofemoralis takes the fourth and fifth caudal transverse processes — a countable segmental address, which makes this one of the few attachment sites that can be scored by position along the column rather than by bone alone.
Proximal carpal between radiale and ulnare, retained in salamanders and reduced or fused in most amniotes. Serially corresponds to the tarsal intermedium but is a separate element.
Proximal tarsal between tibiale and fibulare. Serial counterpart of the carpal intermedium; separate element for the same reason radiale and tibiale are separate.
Central tarsal of the primitive tetrapod ankle, retained in salamanders.
Distal tarsal row. Origin of the intrinsic pedal muscles — the serial counterpart of the distal carpal row in the manus.

An anteroposterior ridge on the lateroventral coracoid, most prominent anteriorly. Named by Walker (1972) and treated as homologous across early crocodylomorphs by Crush (1980); Bodenham et al. report it in Galahadosuchus and compare it with Terrestrisuchus and Dromicosuchus. Scored only for the stem column because no source here identifies it in crown Crocodylia.

A circular depression near the posterior margin of the lateroventral coracoid, present in Galahadosuchus, Dromicosuchus (NCSM 13733) and Terrestrisuchus. Crush (1980) read it as the coracobrachialis anterior attachment.
